newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan MOF says to watch market rates, BOJ response.
newsitem.headline: Japan MOF says to watch market rates, BOJ response.

text.p: Japan's Ministry of Finance will watch movements in market interest rates and also monitor the way in which the Bank of Japan deals with the recent rise in money market rates, Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said on Tuesday.
Asked about the recent rise in money market rates, Mitsuzuka told a news conference: "It is the responsibility of the Bank of Japan. We will watch what they do (about the rise)."
Mitsuzuka said Monday's report implying that he had hinted at a further rise in Japan's consumption tax was regrettable.
He added that he did not intend to consider a tax rise until the year 2005.
"If we push ahead with administrative and fiscal reform then at least until 2005 we will not hold discussions with a tax rise in mind," Mitsuzuka said.
On Monday, Japan's Jiji news agency quoted Mitsuzuka as saying he could not deny the possibility of another tax increase in the future after a scheduled hike on April 1.

Markets interpreted the report as pointing to a possible early rise in the tax and Japanese stocks fell sharply as a result. But the Finance Ministry said later on Monday that Mitsuzuka had not said he was considering a further imminent rise in the consumption tax rate.
Mitsuzuka himself said on Tuesday that the report was misleading.
Mitsuzuka also said four ministries and the prefectural governments of Tokyo and Osaka would meet later on Tuesday to finalise proposals to boost land liquidity.

He said the finance, construction, land and justice ministries, along with the prefectural governments, were expected to approve a package to securitise land held as collateral as well as measures to use such collateralised land to benefit local communities.
The measures are due to be adopted officially as a government plan on March 31.

Mitsuzuka said the collateralised land would be sold to investors, through trust banks, in small lots as securities, in order to boost land liquidity. Regulatory changes will be made by April to allow this approach to be used, he said.
He added that another method, which would allow banks to use special-purpose companies to issue securities backed by collateralised land, would be introduced in fiscal 1998/99.
